design_detail: Retrospective interview case series. Ten people formerly dependent on heroin, attending one methadone maintenance clinic in the New York City area and with a hospital admission for drug overdose in their medical records, were each asked to recount the events of that overdose, on average 5 years after it. The author sorted the accounts by whether the circumstances of drug use had been unusual. No comparison group and no comparison occasions. Presented as a check, in people, of a rat experiment by the same author's group (Siegel et al., 1982) in which heroin given in an unfamiliar environment was more often lethal.
can_establish: That 7 of these 10 survivors of a hospital-treated overdose, asked years later, described something unusual about the occasion, which is consistent with, but does not test, the conditioning account of overdose.
cannot_establish: Whether unusual circumstances raise the risk of overdose (there is no comparison with the same people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose, and the author notes that the frequency of unusual circumstances without overdose is unknown), whether conditioning caused any overdose, or anything about overdose deaths, since only survivors were interviewed.

sample.recruitment: Clinic sample: people attending a methadone maintenance facility in the metropolitan New York City area whose medical records showed a hospital admission for drug overdose (p. 429, METHOD). How the 10 were chosen from those eligible, and how many were approached or declined, is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Former heroin dependence (in methadone maintenance at interview) and a recorded hospital admission for drug overdose. No exclusion criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: 8 men and 2 women; mean age at interview 28 years; mean time from first heroin use to the overdose 5 years (range 2 to 10); mean time from the overdose to the interview 5 years (p. 429, METHOD). Ethnicity, education, other drug use and the dates of the overdoses and interviews are not reported (the manuscript was received in April 1984, p. 430).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); all 10 accounts are reported.
sample.selection_effects: Survivors only, all later in methadone maintenance at one clinic, interviewed about 5 years after the event: people who died, who were not taken to hospital or who never entered treatment are not represented. Recollections years later, by people who knew they were being asked about the overdose, may favour distinctive details; whether the interviewer knew the hypothesis is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Unstructured self-report: each person was asked to recount, in as much detail as possible, the sequence of events on the occasion of the overdose (p. 429, METHOD). The interviews were conducted by H. Berkley (acknowledgment, p. 428). No criteria for judging circumstances typical or atypical are given, and there was no second rater.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: All accounts describe injected heroin; amount and purity unknown. No toxicology.
exposure.polysubstance: Two of the seven atypical accounts concern other drugs: one person took a barbiturate mixture (Tuinal) with the heroin, against his usual practice of using no other drug with it; another, who usually injected cocaine together with heroin, injected heroin alone for the first time in over 9 months because no cocaine was available (p. 429, RESULTS). Other drug use on the occasion was not asked about systematically or verified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; all were in methadone maintenance at interview.

comparison.controls: None. Neither the same people's ordinary occasions of use nor people who used heroin without overdosing were studied.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance at the time of the overdose, the amount and purity of the heroin, time since last use and other drugs taken were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Open-ended interview about the overdose occasion; hospital admission for overdose taken from the medical records.
outcomes.validity_norms: No structured instrument and no reliability check; the medical records served only to confirm that an overdose admission had occurred.
outcomes.operationalization: An account counted as atypical when the person described something different from usual on the overdose occasion: a place never used before, an unusual injection procedure, an unusual drug combination or the absence of a usually combined drug, or an unusually large group in a place not used before (p. 429, RESULTS). No definition was set in advance.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (counts only; no statistical test).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the classification appears to be the author's.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts only. 7 of 10 described atypical circumstances (editors' calculation: 70%, exact binomial 95% CI 35% to 93%): 2 used in places they had never injected in before; 2 described unusual injection procedures; 1 combined heroin with a barbiturate mixture against his usual practice; 1 injected heroin without his usual cocaine; 1 used with a large group in his own living room at his wedding celebration, where he alone overdosed from the shared supply. 3 of 10 recalled no distinctive features of the occasion (p. 429, RESULTS and DISCUSSION).
analysis.selective_reporting: The author concedes that the barbiturate case may reflect a drug interaction and that the three people who recalled nothing distinctive suggest a nonassociative basis (p. 429, DISCUSSION, 1st paragraph). The two unusual-injection accounts (an easy first-attempt injection after usual difficulty finding a vein; a dilution error that meant two injections instead of one) are counted as atypical circumstances; whether they also changed the amount of drug delivered is not discussed.
analysis.power: Not applicable (10 cases, no hypothesis test).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Seven of 10 survivors of a hospital-treated overdose recalled something unusual about that occasion and three recalled nothing distinctive; there is no information on how often the same people used heroin in unusual circumstances without overdosing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the retrospective reports "congenial with these animal data" and extends the suggestion from survivors to overdose death (p. 428). The discussion is more careful: the reports do not prove a conditioning mechanism, large doses and drug interactions also contribute, one case may be a drug interaction, three cases suggest a nonassociative basis, and the frequency of unusual circumstances without overdose is unknown (p. 429). It still calls two cases (the missing cocaine; the wedding) especially compelling. Of the seven atypical accounts, three concern an unfamiliar place or company (the manipulation in the rat experiment), two concern injection technique and two concern which drugs were taken; the last four fit the model only under a broader reading of what counts as a drug cue.

timeline.event: Siegel: in rats, morphine analgesic tolerance was weaker when the last injection was given with cues that had not previously signalled the drug (as cited, p. 428; Siegel, 1976; Siegel & MacRae, 1984).

Siegel, Hinson, Krank & McCully (Science): rats with the same heroin history were more likely to survive a high intravenous heroin dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin than in a different environment (as described, p. 429; survival figures are not given in this paper).
This paper: retrospective accounts from 10 overdose survivors in methadone maintenance.

The author's review of the conditioning account restates situation-specific tolerance, including tolerance to lethal effects in many species, without citing this interview study or other human overdose data

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no later study of the circumstances of overdoses was among the papers read for this card. The paper is a small, uncontrolled set of recollections offered as consistent with an animal finding; it cannot show that unfamiliar settings raise overdose risk in people. The author's own 2005 review of the conditioning account does not cite it.

funding.funder: Grants from the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (p. 428, first-page footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author (McMaster University) whose own animal research supplies the model being checked; the interviews were conducted by H. Berkley. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A case-crossover study of fatal and non-fatal overdoses that compares each person's overdose occasion with that person's own recent occasions of use, with the circumstances (place, company, route, other drugs) recorded by structured interview soon after the event, toxicology for amount and co-ingested drugs, and ideally a marker of tolerance.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Survivors in methadone maintenance at one clinic; people who overdose and die, or who are never treated, are not represented, yet the abstract speaks of overdose death.
How the 10 were selected from eligible clinic attendees is not described.
Ten people; the 95% interval for 7 of 10 runs from 35% to 93% (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Sex, mean age, years of use before the overdose, years since the overdose and the setting are given; dates, other drug use and the severity of the overdoses are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 10 accounts are reported and classified.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The overdose was confirmed from medical records, but the circumstances came from open-ended recall about 5 years later, classified without stated definitions.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Unstructured interviews; a single, unnamed classifier; no reliability check.
Simple counts suit 10 cases, but no interval is given and there is no comparison against which the count could mean anything.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: The number approached and the number who declined are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI prevalence checklist is used because the result is a descriptive count (how many overdose survivors recalled unusual circumstances). The count rests on 10 recollections from one clinic, classified without definitions or a second rater and with no comparison occasions, so it is a weak description and gives no estimate of risk. Cite it for what these survivors recalled and for the author's own caveats, never as evidence that unfamiliar settings cause overdose in people.

key_findings.finding: Ten people formerly dependent on heroin (8 men, 2 women; mean age at interview 28) attending a methadone maintenance clinic in the New York City area, each with a hospital admission for drug overdose in their medical records, were interviewed on average 5 years after the overdose; on average they had used heroin for 5 years (range 2 to 10) before it.
Seven of the 10 described the circumstances of drug use on the occasion of the overdose as atypical.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 70%, exact binomial 95% CI 35% to 93%. No comparison with ordinary occasions of use.

key_findings.finding: The seven atypical accounts: two had injected in places they had never used before (a car-wash bathroom, a candy-store basement); two described unusual injection procedures (one found a vein at the first attempt, unlike her usual difficulty; one diluted the heroin too much, so that two injections instead of the usual one preceded the overdose); one took a barbiturate mixture (Tuinal) with the heroin, against his usual practice; one, who usually injected cocaine with heroin, injected heroin alone for the first time in over 9 months because no cocaine was available; one, after about 10 years of heroin use, used with a large group in his own living room at his wedding celebration, and he alone overdosed from the shared supply.
key_findings.locator: RESULTS (one paragraph, left column, continuing at the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: Three of the 10 could not recall any distinctive feature of the overdose occasion, which the author reads as suggesting a nonassociative basis for their overdoses.

The author states that these retrospective reports do not prove that conditioning is involved in human overdose, that many factors contribute, including unusually large doses and drug interactions, that the barbiturate case may be an adverse drug combination, and that it is unknown how often people use heroin in unusual circumstances without harm.

The study was framed by a rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982): rats with identical heroin histories given a high intravenous dose in the environment previously paired with heroin were more likely to survive than rats given the same final dose in a different environment. Survival figures are not given in this paper.
key_findings.locator: Unheaded introduction, last paragraph before METHOD (left column)

key_findings.finding: The conditioning model as stated: cues present when a drug is taken become associated with its effects; the conditional responses they come to elicit are often opposite in direction to the drug's effects, attenuate those effects and contribute to tolerance. Tolerance should therefore fail when the drug is taken in an environment not previously paired with it, and in rats morphine tolerance was weaker when the last injection came with unfamiliar cues (Siegel, 1976; Siegel & MacRae, 1984).
key_findings.locator: Unheaded introduction, 2nd paragraph (p. 428) and 3rd paragraph (begins p. 428, right column, ends at the top of p. 429)

key_findings.finding: Background cited from older sources: about 1% of people dependent on heroin die each year, mostly from an acute reaction to injected heroin (Maurer & Vogel, 1973); many such deaths follow a dose that would not be expected to be fatal for a tolerant person (reviews by Brecher, 1972, and Reed, 1980), sometimes a dose tolerated the day before (Government of Canada, 1973).
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures from 1970s sources; not a current estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the reports suggest that the model may be relevant to some overdose deaths, but only survivors were interviewed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper says nothing directly about deaths; claims should say survivors.

reporting_issues.issue: No definition of an atypical circumstance was set in advance, no second rater classified the accounts, and whether the interviewer knew the hypothesis is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of 7 of 10 reflects one classifier's reading of open-ended recollections.

reporting_issues.issue: The 7 atypical accounts combine changes of setting or company (3), of injection technique (2) and of which drugs were taken (2); only the first match the environmental manipulation of the rat experiment.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim that 7 of 10 overdosed in an unfamiliar place would overstate the data: 3 of 10 described an unfamiliar place or company.
